info.desc: "Heroes" is an album by David Bowie, released in 1977. The second installment of his "Berlin Trilogy" with Brian Eno (the other releases being "Low" and "Lodger") "Heroes" developed the sound of "Low" in a more positive direction. Of the three albums, it was the most befitting of the appellation "Berlin", being the only one wholly recorded there. The title track remains one of Bowie's best known, a classic story of two lovers who meet at the Berlin Wall. The album is considered one of his best by critics, notably for the contributions of guitarist Robert Fripp who flew in .

podcast.body: Released in 1977, this album is described as the best known of the three albums Bowie made while influenced by Krautrock during his time in Berlin. The title track is highlighted, and its B-side, "V-2 Schneider," was explicitly named after Kraftwerk's Florian Schneider, underscoring the direct inspiration. "The best known of those is probably heroes from 1977."

podcast.body: An experimental album from Bowie's Berlin period that, like other Berlin LPs, consistently made the UK Top 5 but fell short of the Top 10 in America. Its famous black and white album cover, depicting Bowie holding his hands around his face in a "proto-vogue pose," was later satirized for "The Next Day" album cover. "Bowie's lowest charter since the experimental heroes a decade earlier."

podcast.body: David Bowie created this album, along with two others, in Berlin with producer Brian Eno. These works were notably Kraftwerk-inspired and demonstrated Bowie's exploration of electronics-driven music as a potential future direction for rock. "He created three craftwork inspired albums with producer Brian Eno that show that maybe electronics were the way for."

podcast.body: Recorded at Hansa Studio, this album continued Bowie's exploration of Krautrock influences, with its title attributed to a song by the German band Neu! and featuring "V2 Schneider" as a tribute to Florian Schneider of Kraftwerk. Released ten months after "Low," it contained the earliest elements of what would become New Wave music and is historically recognized as one of Bowie's all-time best records. "Heroes was also recorded at Hansa. Bowie continued to follow his Crout Rock Muse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 2

podcast.body: Recorded at Hansa Studios, just 500 meters from the Berlin Wall, this album saw Bowie in a better mental state, aiming for a more optimistic vibe. It featured producer Tony Visconti, crucial collaboration from Brian Eno, and the same band from *Low*. Robert Fripp later joined, surprising Bowie and Visconti with his enthusiasm and adaptability, helping to define the album's epic atmosphere and creating unique sound textures. Visconti considered it a more positive version of *Low*, maintaining the structure of a conventional song side and an ambient/instrumental side. It was better received than its predecessor. "En esa época, Bowie se encontraba en un mejor estado mental, por lo que quería una hire más optimista para el disco."

podcast.body: Recorded in Berlin in 1977, this album features the title track which received special treatment from King Crimson guitarist Robert Fripp. Fripp was instructed to "do something weird," leading him to create three feedback loops using his guitar at different distances from the amplifier, which were then fed through an EMS synthesizer. The album also utilized piano, a special microphone setup, early synthesizers, and a Chamberlain keyboard. "Bowie was in Berlin working on what would become his hero's album, and the title track needed some special treatment."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Distortion and Feedback

podcast.body: Recorded less than ten months after "Low" at Hansa Studio, this album continued Bowie's exploration of "crowd rock" and electronic sounds. Its title is a tribute to a song by the German band Neu!, and it includes "V2 Schneider," a nod to Florian Schneider of Kraftwerk. The record captured the nascent elements of what would become New Wave music, with Bowie once again ahead of trends. It is widely considered one of his all-time best records. "Heroes has gone down in history as one of Bowie's all time best records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 2

podcast.body: Similar to "Low," "Heroes" also features a second part that is largely instrumental. This side heavily recalls Brian Eno's concurrent solo projects and his collaborations with artists like Cluster from the late 1970s, although Bowie also significantly contributed to these instrumental sections.

podcast.body: The release of "Heroes" was significantly smoother than "Low," largely due to the unexpected success of its predecessor, which made RCA more receptive to Bowie's experimental projects in Germany. The album was seen as having more commercial potential, and RCA heavily invested in its promotion, using the famous advertising slogan: "There's Old Wave, there's New Wave, and there's David Bowie," positioning him as a pioneer of fresh, new music.

srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 2

podcast.body: The second album in Bowie's Berlin trilogy, arriving nine months after 'Low' in 1977, is best remembered for its title track, now considered one of Bowie's most cherished songs and called his "masterpiece." Though initially underrated and a modest performer (peaking at #35 on Billboard LPs), it depicted lovers by the Berlin Wall during the Cold War with innovative production by Tony Visconti, oscillating electronics by Brian Eno, and guitar drone by Robert Fripp. "Heroes has been called David Boey's masterpiece."

podcast.body: The second album in the "Berlin Trilogy," created with Brian Eno. It emerged from a period of intense personal and artistic transformation for Bowie, following his move to Berlin to address his drug addiction.

podcast.body: The third album in David Bowie's Berlin trilogy was titled "Heroes." It was recorded at Hansa Studios, which was located within sight of the infamous Berlin Wall. The title track of the album was reportedly inspired by Bowie observing two strangers sharing a kiss by the Wall, adding a poignant, human element to the backdrop of Cold War division. "The third of Bowie's Berlin albums was called Heroes."

The entire record was made in Studio Two of Hansa Studios, a location about 150 yards from the Berlin Wall, which added to the album's distinct atmosphere. srcs.episode: Stories Behind Songs - 5

podcast.body: Unlike "Low," "Heroes" is rich with continuous lyrical and thematic references to Germany and Berlin. These include allusions to the Berlin Wall, the divided city, the communist era, and the lack of freedom in the communist sector. This strong thematic connection to the city solidifies its reputation as the "heart of the Berlin Trilogy."

podcast.body: Work on "Heroes" began almost immediately after "Low" was published in 1977. It is widely considered the true "Berlin album" of the trilogy, being the only one recorded entirely in Berlin. The recording process was very rapid, completed in just a few weeks, indicative of the strong working relationship between Bowie and Brian Eno, who had a clear vision.
